text:
The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers' housing costs (CPIH) rose by 2.8% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 3.0% the previous month.

On a monthly basis, CPIH rose by 0.2% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% in June 2025.

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 2.6% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 2.8% the previous month.

On a monthly basis, CPI rose by 0.1% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% in June 2025.

Transport, and food and non-alcoholic beverages made the largest downward contributions to the monthly change in both CPIH and CPI annual rates.

Core CPIH (CPIH excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) rose by 2.8% in the 12 months to June 2026, unchanged from the 12 months to May; the CPIH goods annual rate slowed from 2.0% to 1.7%, while the CPIH services annual rate was unchanged, at 3.6%.

Core CPI (CPI excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) rose by 2.6% in the 12 months to June 2026, unchanged from the 12 months to May; the CPI goods annual rate slowed from 2.0% to 1.7%, while the CPI services annual rate eased from 3.7% to 3.6%.

text:
The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers' housing costs (CPIH) rose by 2.8% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 3.0% the previous month (Figure 1). The 12-month rate for June was the lowest recorded since September 2024, when it was 2.6%.

On a monthly basis, CPIH rose by 0.2% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% in June 2025.

The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 2.6% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 2.8% the previous month. The 12-month rate was also 2.6% in March 2025 and it was last lower in December 2024, when it was 2.5%.

On a monthly basis, CPI rose by 0.1% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% in June 2025.

The main drivers of the annual inflation rate for CPIH and CPI are the same where they are common to both measures. However, the owner occupiers' housing (OOH) costs component accounts for approximately 18% of the CPIH and is the main driver for differences between the CPIH and CPI inflation rates.

This makes CPIH our most comprehensive measure of inflation. We cover this in more detail in Section 4: Latest movements in CPIH inflation and provide a commentary on the CPI in Section 5: Latest movements in CPI inflation . We also cover both CPIH and CPI in Section 3: Notable movements in prices , though the figures reflect CPIH.

text:
Individual contributions may not sum to the total because of rounding.

More information on the contents of each division can be found in Table 3 of our Consumer price inflation dataset .

Figure 2 shows the contributions from the 12 divisions to the change in the annual Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers' housing costs (CPIH) inflation rate between May and June 2026. These sum to the change in the annual rate, from 3.0% to 2.8%, between these months.

The decrease in the 12-month rate between May and June 2026 reflected downward contributions from five divisions, partially offset by upward contributions from three divisions. The largest downward contribution came from transport, particularly motor fuels. There were no large, offsetting upward contributions.

Prices in the transport division rose overall by 5.7% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 6.8% the previous month (Figure 3). On a monthly basis, prices fell by 0.3% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.7% a year ago.

The largest downward effect behind the slowing in the transport annual rate came from motor fuels, particularly diesel.

The average price of diesel fell by 10.7 pence per litre between May and June 2026, compared with a fall of 0.6 pence per litre between May and June 2025. The average price stood at 176.4 pence per litre in June 2026.

Petrol prices fell by 2.1 pence per litre in June 2026, compared with a fall of 0.5 pence per litre in June 2025. The average price stood at 155.3 pence per litre in June 2026. This is the first time petrol prices have eased since the start of the conflict in the Middle East, on 28 February 2026.

These movements resulted in overall motor fuel prices rising by 21.3% in the 12 months to June 2026, compared with a rise of 24.6% in the 12 months to May, which was the highest recorded rate since September 2022.

text:
Within transport, there was a smaller downward effect from vehicle maintenance and repair. Prices fell by 0.2% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 2.0% in June 2025. The movements were caused by price changes for roadside recovery services.

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 1.7% in the 12 months to June 2026, down from 2.2% the previous month (Figure 4). The annual rate in June was the lowest since August 2024, when it was 1.3%. On a monthly basis, food and non-alcoholic beverage prices fell by 0.2% in June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3% a year ago.

There were small downward effects behind the change in the annual rate from 5 of the 11 detailed classes. The largest of these effects came from sugar, jam, syrups, chocolate and confectionery, for which prices of chocolate fell by more in June 2026 than June 2025. This class made a downward contribution of 0.02 percentage points to the change in the CPIH inflation rate.

Other slightly smaller downward effects came from oils and fats (particularly margarine and other vegetable oils), meat (particularly beef), dairy, and vegetables. Prices of oils and fats, and dairy, fell in June 2026, compared with a price rise and little change a year ago, respectively. Meat and vegetable prices rose in June 2026 but by less than in June 2025.

The other six detailed classes within food and non-alcoholic beverages had little effect on the change in the headline rate. These were bread and cereals, fish, fruit, other food products, hot beverages, and soft drinks.

Clothing and footwear prices fell by 0.5% in the 12 months to June 2026, compared with a rise of 0.2% the previous month.

text:
On a monthly basis, prices fell by 1.2% in June 2026, compared with a smaller fall of 0.4% in June 2025. Prices tend to fall in June as the summer sales season begins, and the movements reflect changes in the proportion of discounted prices in the datasets. This proportion rose between May and June this year by more than the rise seen over the same period a year ago.
